notes.28:13: Greek lists all twelve gemstones of the high priest's breastpiece (cf. Exod 28:17-20) along with silver and gold, whereas the Hebrew MT lists nine stones.
notes.28:14: Greek reads "with the cherub" (meta tou cheroub), distinguishing the ruler of Tyre from the cherub who leads him out in v. 16, whereas the Hebrew MT reads "you were an anointed guardian cherub." In v. 15 Greek reads "in your days" (MT "in your ways"), and in v. 18 "I profaned" (MT "you profaned").
notes.29:1: The Greek text dates this oracle to the twelfth year, tenth month, first day, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has the tenth year, tenth month, twelfth day.
notes.29:4: Greek pagidas ("snares") and pterygas ("fins", literally "wings") differ from the Hebrew text's "hooks" and "scales"; in v. 5, the Greek also reads "quickly" (en tachei) where Hebrew has "into the wilderness".
notes.29:7: The Greek reads "when every hand clapped against them" (ekrotēsen ep' autous pasa cheir), diverging from the Hebrew text ("you tore open every shoulder for them").
notes.29:10: Greek rhomphaian ("sword") reflects reading the Hebrew consonants for "drought/desolation" as "sword"; "Ethiopians" renders Greek Aithiopes, the Septuagint name corresponding to Hebrew Cush (also "Ethiopia" in 30:4, 9).
notes.29:19: "The Lord, the Lord" translates the doubled Greek title kyrios Kyrios (corresponding to Hebrew Adonai YHWH), which also appears at the end of v. 20 introducing v. 21 in the Greek text.
notes.30:5: The Greek lists "Persians and Cretans and Lydians and Libyans" (differing from the Hebrew list beginning with Cush and Put) and reads "some of the sons of My covenant" (tōn huiōn tēs diathēkēs mou).
notes.30:13: The Greek reads "nobles from Memphis and rulers of Memphis" where Hebrew has "idols" and "a prince"; "Memphis" is the Greek city name corresponding to Hebrew Noph.
notes.30:14: "Tanis" and "Diospolis" are the Septuagint's Greek city names for Hebrew Zoan and No (Thebes), just as "Sais" (v. 15), "Heliopolis", and "Bubastis" (v. 17) correspond to Hebrew Sin, Aven/On, and Pi-beseth.
notes.30:16: "Waters will be poured out" (diachythēsetai hydata) is a notable Septuagint reading where the Hebrew text speaks of Memphis having daily adversaries.
notes.30:21: The Greek has plural "arms" (singular in Hebrew) and the verb katedeēthē, a variant passive form of katadeō ("bind up", though formally resembling katadeomai, "ask for"); in v. 22, the Greek describes the arms as "strong and outstretched" rather than "strong and broken".
notes.31:3: Greek kyparissos ("cypress") corresponds to Hebrew "cedar", and "clouds" (nephelōn, also in vv. 10, 14) reflects reading the Hebrew consonants as "clouds" rather than "thick boughs".
notes.31:8: The Greek lacks a negative in the opening clause ("such cypresses were in the paradise of God"), unlike the Hebrew ("cedars could not rival it in the garden of God"). In v. 9 (and vv. 16, 18), "delight" (tryphē) translates Hebrew Eden.
notes.31:10: The Greek shifts from second person to third person and reads "I saw when it was exalted" (eidon en tō hypsōthēnai auton) where the Hebrew text has "its heart was lifted up in its height".
notes.31:14: The middle clauses in Greek shift to indicative verbs ("and they put their top into the midst of clouds, and they did not stand in their height beside them"), differing from the continued negative purpose clause in Hebrew.
notes.31:17: "Hades" (vv. 15-17) is the Septuagint's Greek name for Hebrew Sheol; here the Greek also reads "its seed" (sperma, vs. Hebrew "arm") and "perished in the midst of their life" (vs. Hebrew "in the midst of the nations").
notes.32:1: The Greek dates this oracle to the tenth month (whereas the Hebrew reads the twelfth month); similarly, v. 17 specifies the first month where the Hebrew omits the month.
notes.32:8: Greek kyrios Kyrios ("the Lord, the Lord") doubles kyrios to represent the Hebrew compound divine title (Adonai YHWH) without adding theos ("God"), a recurring idiom in Septuagint Ezekiel.
notes.32:20: Greek traumatias literally means "wounded one" and is regularly used in the Septuagint for those mortally wounded or slain in battle. Verse 19 is absent as a separate verse in the Greek, with its wording appearing in v. 21.
notes.32:21: Greek reads "in the depth of tumult" (thorybou), likely an early inner-Greek transposition of bothrou ("pit").
notes.32:29: Here and in v. 30 the Greek reads "Assyria" (Assour) where the Hebrew names Edom (v. 29) and the Sidonians (v. 30). Also in v. 27 the Greek reads positively ("they lay down with the giants"), lacking the Hebrew negation.
notes.33:13: The Greek omits the Hebrew clause "he shall surely live," placing "This one has trusted in his righteousness" directly after "When I say to the righteous one."
notes.33:21: The Greek dates the survivor's arrival to the twelfth month, whereas the Hebrew reads the tenth month.
notes.33:25: The Greek moves directly from the messenger formula here to the oath in v. 27, omitting the indictments found in the Hebrew of vv. 25b-26.
notes.33:27: Greek thanato ("with death") reflects the Septuagint's standard rendering of Hebrew deber ("pestilence").
notes.34:2: Greek repeats the title kyrios Kyrios ("the Lord, the Lord"), representing the Hebrew formula Adonai YHWH. Unlike the Hebrew MT ("Woe, shepherds of Israel who have been feeding themselves"), the Greek begins with a vocative ("O shepherds of Israel") followed by two rhetorical questions.
notes.34:3: Greek reads "the milk" (to gala), reflecting the Hebrew consonantal text vocalized as chalav ("milk") rather than MT chelev ("fat").
notes.34:16: Greek reads "and the strong I will guard" (phylaxo, reflecting Hebrew shmr "guard"), whereas the Hebrew MT reads "and the fat and the strong I will destroy" (shmd).
notes.34:25: Greek explicitly names "David" ("I will make with David a covenant of peace"), whereas the Hebrew MT reads "with them."
notes.34:29: Greek reads "a plant of peace" (phyton eirenes, reflecting Hebrew shalom), whereas the Hebrew MT reads "a planting of renown" (leshem).
notes.35:5: Greek reads "lay in wait for the house of Israel with deceit, by the hand of enemies with a sword," diverging substantially from the Hebrew MT ("delivered the sons of Israel to the power of the sword").
notes.35:6: Greek has a notably shorter text than the Hebrew MT and reads literally "you have sinned against [or 'with respect to'] blood" (eis haima hemartes).
notes.35:7: Greek reads "people and livestock" (anthropous kai ktene), where the Hebrew MT reads "the one who passes through and returns."
notes.35:15: Greek uses the Hellenistic geographical name "Idumea" (Idoumaia, corresponding to Hebrew Edom), adds "and it will be completely consumed" (reading Hebrew klh as a verb rather than "all of it"), and closes with the singular "you will know" plus "their God."
notes.36:2: Greek doubles the divine title (kyrios Kyrios, "the Lord, the Lord") here and elsewhere in Ezekiel to render Hebrew Adonai YHWH. Greek also reads erema aionia ("everlasting wastes") where the Hebrew MT has "ancient heights."
notes.36:5: Greek uses Idoumaia ("Idumea"), the Hellenistic geographical name corresponding to Edom in the Hebrew text. The closing clause ("dishonoring souls so as to lay waste in plunder") reflects a distinct Septuagint reading.
notes.36:31: The Greek text has third-person plural pronouns ("before their face" and "over their abominations") where the Hebrew MT reads second-person plural ("your").
notes.36:33: Here and in 36:37 the Greek text retains the Hebrew transliteration Adonai before Kyrios ("Adonai the Lord"), marking a notable translational shift within 36:23b-38.
notes.36:35: Greek translates Hebrew Eden by its sense as kepos tryphes ("a garden of delight") rather than transliterating it as a proper name.
notes.37:1: The Greek text makes Kyrios ("the Lord") the nominative subject ("the Lord brought me out in the Spirit"), reads pedion ("plain") rather than "valley," and specifies anthropinon ("human") bones.
notes.37:9: Throughout 37:1-14 Greek uses the single noun pneuma for God's Spirit (including "My Spirit" in v. 6, where the MT lacks "My"), animating spirit or breath (vv. 5, 8-10), and the "four winds" (v. 9).
notes.37:10: Greek reads synagoge ("assembly"), where the Hebrew MT has "army."
notes.37:19: Greek uses phyle ("tribe") rather than "stick" for Joseph and Judah, and concludes "in the hand of Judah" where the Hebrew MT reads "in My hand."
notes.37:22: Greek uses archon ("ruler") here and in vv. 24-25, whereas the Hebrew MT has "king" in vv. 22, 24 and "prince" in v. 25.
notes.38:2: The Greek treats Rosh as a proper name alongside Meshech and Tubal (whereas the Hebrew term is sometimes understood as 'chief') and reads 'Gog and the land of Magog.'
notes.38:3: The Septuagint double title kyrios Kyrios ('the Lord, the Lord') renders the Hebrew compound title Adonai YHWH and recurs in 38:10, 17, 18; 39:8, 25, 29.
notes.38:11: The Greek reads 'a cast-off land' (gen aperrimmenen), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's 'land of unwalled villages.'
notes.38:13: The Greek uses the distinct proper name 'Carthaginian' (Karchedonioi) where the Hebrew has 'Tarshish,' and reads 'villages' (komai) where the Hebrew has 'young lions.'
notes.38:21: The Greek reads 'against it even every terror' (ep' auto kai pan phobon), diverging from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's 'for a sword against him on all my mountains.'
notes.39:12: 'Te' (Greek To te, a variant transcription of Hebrew ge, 'valley'; compare 'Gai' in 39:15) is paired with polyandrion ('Burial Ground,' literally 'place of many men,' also the city name in 39:16), which translates Hebrew Hamon ('multitude') as a common burial site.
notes.39:18: The Greek renders the Hebrew term for mighty warriors as 'giants' (giganton; also singular giganta in 39:20) and omits 'of Bashan.'
notes.39:21: The Greek reads 'among you' (en hymin), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'among the nations.'
notes.39:28: The Greek concludes with 'when I appear to them among the nations' (en to epiphanenai me autois en tois ethnesin), lacking the longer Masoretic statement about sending Israel into exile and leaving none behind.
notes.39:29: The Greek reads 'My fury' (ton thymon mou), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'My Spirit.'
notes.40:7: Throughout chapter 40, the Greek retains transliterated Hebrew architectural terms: thee/theeim (and here the unique form thaielatha) rendered 'guardroom(s)', ailam rendered 'porch', ailammon rendered 'vestibule(s)', and ail/aileu rendered 'jamb(s)'. In vv. 7-8, the Greek text explicitly measures three guardrooms in sequence.
notes.40:17: The Greek text reads 'the inner court' (as also in v. 34) and 'colonnades' (peristyla), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'the outer court' and 'pavement'.
notes.40:31: Verse 30 is absent from the Greek text, so the final clause of v. 29 runs directly into the genitive phrase 'of the porch toward the outer court' at the beginning of v. 31.
notes.40:38: Verses 38-40 follow a distinctive Greek text mentioning 'the second gate', a 'drain' (ekrysis), and 'the channel of the burnt offerings' (rhoax), with v. 39 omitting the porch tables described in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.40:43: The Greek text describes a handbreadth hewn rim and overhead coverings for shelter from rain and dryness, differing substantially from the hooks and sacrificial flesh of the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.41:1: Greek uses the Hebrew architectural loanword ailam ("porch") here and in vv. 2, 15, and 25-26, where the Hebrew of v. 1 refers to pilasters or jambs.
notes.41:4: The Greek reads "the length of the doors, forty cubits," whereas the Hebrew reads "its length, twenty cubits."
notes.41:6: The Greek wording is difficult and diverges from the Hebrew, giving the count literally as "thirty, three times twice" and describing the wall interval as enabling "those taking hold" to see so as not to touch the house walls.
notes.41:8: "Thrael" transliterates an obscure Greek term of uncertain meaning, likely arising from the underlying Hebrew text; in v. 7 the Greek also reads "from the cornices" (geison) rather than "from the middle ones."
notes.41:22: The Greek omits "of the Lord" after "before the face" (found in the Hebrew and some Greek manuscripts), adds the breadth of two cubits, and reads "horns" and "its base."
notes.42:1: The Greek reads "into the inner court toward the east" and "five chambers," where the Hebrew reads "out to the outer court" and a singular "chamber."
notes.42:7: Here and in 41:11 and 42:10-12, the Greek uses phos ("light") for an unroofed space or architectural light opening, where the Hebrew refers to a wall or place.
notes.42:13: The Greek adds "the sons of Zadok" and renders the final offering category as "the offerings for ignorance" (agnoia, where the Hebrew has "guilt offering").
notes.42:14: The Greek differs substantially from the Hebrew, stating that none may enter except the priests, that those who approach may be continually holy, and that their vestments must not be touched.
notes.42:17: The Greek specifies "five hundred cubits" here and in v. 20 (with cubits implied in vv. 16 and 18-19), whereas the Hebrew measures five hundred reeds; in vv. 18-19 the Greek also orders west (lit. "the sea") before south, and in v. 20 reads "the outer wall" (proteichisma) rather than "the common/profane."
notes.43:2: The Greek reads "the sound of the encampment was like the sound of many redoubling" (τῆς παρεμβολῆς ... διπλασιαζόντων πολλῶν), differing notably from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "like the sound of many waters."
notes.43:3: The Greek reads "to anoint the city" (τοῦ χρῖσαι) and "the vision of the chariot" (τοῦ ἅρματος), where the Masoretic Text has "to destroy the city" and "visions."
notes.43:5: Greek πνεῦμα here is anarthrous and can be rendered either "the Spirit" or "a spirit" / "a wind."
notes.43:7: Here and in v. 9 the Greek reads "in the murders of the rulers" (ἐν τοῖς φόνοις τῶν ἡγουμένων), whereas the Masoretic Text refers to "the corpses of their kings."
notes.43:14: The Greek renders the altar's tiers or ledges as ἱλαστήριον ("propitiatory," place of atonement) throughout vv. 14-20, and here reads "this great propitiatory below" before contrasting the small and great propitiatories.
notes.43:15: "Ariel" (ἁριήλ/ἀριήλ) is a Greek transliteration of the Hebrew term for the altar hearth; the Greek also reads "above the horns is a cubit" rather than specifying four horns, and in v. 26 uses "fill their hands," the biblical idiom for consecration or ordination.
notes.44:2: The Greek uses the future tense "will enter" (εἰσελεύσεται), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has the past tense "has entered."
notes.44:3: "Porch" renders αἰλάμ (ailam), a Greek transliteration of the Hebrew architectural term for the porch of the gate.
notes.44:14: The Greek uses the third-person plural "they shall bring them down" (κατάξουσιν), whereas the Masoretic Text has the first-person singular "I will appoint them."
notes.44:20: The Greek reads "strip bare their hair" and "surely cover their heads" (καλύπτοντες καλύψουσιν), differing from the Masoretic Text's command to trim the hair; similarly in v. 18 the Greek reads "by force" (βίᾳ) where the Hebrew refers to sweat.
notes.44:25: "The soul of a person" (ψυχὴν ἀνθρώπου) is a Septuagint idiom denoting a human corpse, corresponding to "a dead person" in the Hebrew.
notes.45:1: The Greek text gives the width as twenty thousand here and in vv. 3 and 5 (where the Hebrew MT reads ten thousand), and leaves the unit of measurement unstated. In v. 5 the Greek likewise reads "cities to live in" where the Hebrew MT has "twenty chambers."
notes.45:12: The Greek uses Greek units of measure and weight—choenix (vv. 10-11), obol (v. 12), and cotyle (v. 14)—and sets the mina at fifty shekels in a compressed numerical sequence (contrast the Hebrew MT's twenty gerahs and sixty-shekel mina).
notes.45:15: The Greek specifies a levy of one sheep out of ten from all the families of Israel (where the Hebrew MT reads one out of two hundred from the well-watered pastures of Israel).
notes.45:20: The Greek prescribes a second sanctuary cleansing on the first day of the seventh month with "a portion from each one" (where the Hebrew MT sets it on the seventh day of the first month for anyone who errs unintentionally).
notes.45:24: Here and in 46:5, 7, 11 the Greek reads "cake" (Greek pemma, a baked offering) where the Hebrew MT reads the dry measure "ephah." In v. 25 and ch. 46 the Greek uses the Hebrew loanword manaa for "grain offering."
notes.46:2: The Greek transliterates Hebrew ulam ("porch") as ailam (also v. 8) and specifies "the inner gate" where the Hebrew MT reads "from outside."
notes.46:12: The Greek joins "freewill offering" and "burnt offering of deliverance" without "or" and uses active verbs so that the ruler himself opens the gate and shuts "the doors."
notes.46:19: The Greek has a singular "chamber of the holy things of the priests" and "a place set apart" (where the Hebrew MT has plural chambers and "at the far western end").
notes.46:20: The Greek renders the guilt offering as "the offerings for ignorance" and uses the adverbial phrase to parapan with the negation ("so as not to carry them out at all").
notes.47:3: In vv. 3-5 the Greek verbs describe the guide himself passing through the stream rather than leading Ezekiel through, and read "water of release" (Greek apheseos) here and "up to the thighs" in v. 4 (where the Hebrew MT has "ankle-deep" and "knee-deep").
notes.47:8: The Greek renders the geographical terms as the proper names "Galilee" and "Arabia" (corresponding to "the eastern region" and "the Arabah" in the Hebrew MT).
notes.47:12: The Greek reads "it shall certainly not grow old," "in its newness it shall bear firstfruits," and "their growth shall be for healing" (where the Hebrew MT speaks of leaves not withering, bearing fruit every month, and leaves for healing).
notes.47:13: The Greek reads "an addition of a measured portion," taking the Hebrew name Yosef ("Joseph") as the verb "to add" (where the Hebrew MT reads "Joseph shall have two portions").
notes.47:16: The Greek border description in vv. 15-20 preserves several Septuagint-distinct place names and renderings—including Seldamma (v. 15), Abthera, Heliam, the court of Saunan, Auranitis (v. 16), Loranitis and Palm Grove (Greek Phoinikon, rendering Tamar in vv. 18-19), and Marimoth-kadem (v. 19)—and vv. 22-23 read "they shall eat in an inheritance" and "in a tribe of proselytes."
notes.48:1: The Greek reads 'the descent of that which cuts around' where the Hebrew has 'the way of Hethlon,' and 'the court of Ailam' as an LXX-distinct proper name where the Hebrew has 'Hazar-enan.'
notes.48:10: The Greek omits the eastern measurement found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and reads 'the mountain of the holy places' (Hebrew: 'the sanctuary of the Lord'). Earlier in v. 9 the Greek also gives a width of twenty-five thousand (and twenty thousand in v. 13) where the Hebrew has ten thousand.
notes.48:15: The Greek renders the Hebrew term for 'common use' with a word meaning 'outer wall' or 'outwork,' apparently reading the similar Hebrew word for a rampart.
notes.48:28: The Greek preserves several distinct geographical readings: 'Teman' (Hebrew: 'Tamar'), the LXX-distinct name 'Barimoth Kadesh' (Hebrew: 'Meribath-kadesh'), and 'of an inheritance' (reading the Hebrew word for 'toward the brook' as 'inheritance').
notes.48:35: Instead of the Hebrew Masoretic Text's city name 'the Lord Is There,' the Greek reflects a different reading and vocalization of the Hebrew consonants, rendering 'from whatever day it comes into being, shall be its name.'
